message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the most important rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. For specific legal advice, consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Tips | |----------|------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a security deposit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after lease ends, unless the landlord provides a written itemized list of deductions.
• Landlord may keep a deposit for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear, or other breaches. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written receipt for the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition**.
• Must repair major structural defects, plumbing, heating, electrical, and ensure proper ventilation. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a habitability issue, you may **repair it yourself** and deduct the cost from your rent, provided the cost is **reasonable** and you give the landlord written notice. | • Keep receipts and proof of the repair.
• The deduction cannot exceed the actual cost of the repair. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords may increase rent at the end of a lease term or with a **30‑day written notice** for month‑to‑month tenants.
• No statutory cap on rent increases (except in certain cities with rent‑control ordinances). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• If you’re in a city with rent control, check local ordinances. | | **Eviction** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** before filing an eviction:
 • 3‑day notice for non‑payment of rent.
 • 30‑day notice for lease termination (month‑to‑month).
 • 60‑day notice for lease termination (fixed‑term).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the notice is improper, consult an attorney. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable notice” means a written notice or a phone call at least 24 hours before entry. | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you may withhold rent or seek damages. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas’ own Fair Housing laws, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • Report discriminatory practices to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • You may terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease (e.g., fails to maintain habitability).
• Some leases include a “break clause” allowing early termination for a fee. | • Provide written notice and document the landlord’s breach. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for: unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, cleaning costs if the unit was left dirty, and any other breaches.
• The landlord must provide an itemized statement if you dispute deductions. | • Dispute any unjustified deductions in writing. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities are the tenant’s responsibility.
• If the landlord fails to provide essential services (heat, hot water, electricity), you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct. | • Keep utility bills and any correspondence. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases require landlord approval for subletting or assignment.
• Texas law does not prohibit subletting, but the lease may restrict it. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • **Small claims court**: You can sue for up to $20,000 for unpaid rent or damages.
• **Tenant‑rights organizations**: Many nonprofits offer free or low‑cost legal assistance. | • Keep all documentation: lease, receipts, correspondence, photos. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand rent amount, due dates, pet policies, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 3 days for non‑payment, 30 days for month‑to‑month termination, 60 days for fixed‑term termination. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Send a written notice to the landlord and keep a copy. 5. **Seek Legal Help Early** – If you face eviction or disputes over deposits, contact a tenant‑rights group or attorney. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** | Guides on tenant rights, dispute resolution. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Complaint filing for discrimination. | https://www.tchra.texas.gov/ | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | National fair housing resources. | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free legal clinics, mediation. | Search “tenant rights organization Texas” + your city. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Process for filing claims up to $20k. | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have strong protections against unfair treatment, unlawful eviction, and unsafe living conditions. By staying informed, keeping records, and knowing the proper procedures, you can assert your rights effectively. If you encounter a problem, act quickly—many remedies (like repair‑and‑deduct or withholding rent) require timely notice. If you need personalized legal advice, consider contacting a local attorney or tenant‑rights nonprofit.
